body:
Parkland Walk succeeds because the railway has not disappeared. The tracks have gone, but the cutting still narrows your view, bridges arrive at railway intervals and old platforms rise beside a path now used by walkers, runners and cyclists. Nature has taken over the infrastructure without making it invisible.

The best-known stretch runs from Finsbury Park towards Highgate. A shorter northern section resumes beyond Highgate Wood and continues towards Alexandra Palace. They are not joined by an accessible tunnel adventure: the former Highgate railway tunnels and track are closed, and the connection between the two public sections follows ordinary streets. That interruption is not a defect to hide. It explains why the walk is both a green corridor and a fragment of unfinished transport history.

## Start at Finsbury Park and let the city fall away

The southern section begins beside Finsbury Park and climbs onto the former track bed. Almost immediately, the route sits above back gardens and roads. You are still in dense north London, but the city is seen through railings, embankments and leaves rather than from the pavement.

The path is broad enough to feel easy, yet it is shared. Fast bicycles, dogs and runners can puncture the illusion of solitude on a sunny weekend. Early morning, a weekday or a less perfect day gives the railway details more room. After prolonged rain, expect mud and standing water rather than a manicured park surface.

Do not hurry through the first kilometres simply to reach the abandoned stations. Brick retaining walls, bridge abutments and changes from embankment to cutting show the engineering decisions that made the line possible across hilly ground. The route’s calm comes from those decisions: the railway created a long space protected from much of the surrounding traffic.

## Crouch End station is still legible

The surviving platforms at Crouch End provide the walk’s clearest moment of railway archaeology. They are overgrown and incomplete, but the relationship between platform, bridge and track bed can still be read without a reconstruction. Stand between them and the width of the old railway suddenly becomes obvious.

The line began as a Great Northern Railway route in the nineteenth century. The branch to Alexandra Palace opened in 1873, designed to carry visitors to the new entertainment complex on the hill. In the late 1930s, part of the route was intended for the Northern Heights extension of the Underground. War, changing transport patterns and the post-war Green Belt undermined the plan. The last passenger train ran in 1954; limited railway use continued until 1970, and the tracks were lifted the following year.

That sequence matters. Parkland Walk is not simply an ancient railway abandoned in one clean moment. It records a line built for Victorian expansion, partly prepared for an Underground future and then made obsolete before that future arrived.

## The Spriggan is newer than the ruins

Near the Crouch End platforms, look up at the brickwork rather than only along the path. The Spriggan—a large, unsettling figure emerging from an arch—has become Parkland Walk’s unofficial guardian. It looks as though it has occupied the railway for a century, but artist Marilyn Collins created it in 1993.

That date corrects a persistent piece of London folklore. The sculpture did not inspire Stephen King’s story *Crouch End*; his story predates it. The Spriggan works because it is a modern intervention that understands the atmosphere already present: damp brick, high vegetation and the feeling of a route removed from the streets above.

The surrounding walls also carry changing layers of graffiti. Some visitors treat them as damage, others as part of the corridor’s urban life. Either way, the contrast prevents the walk from becoming a sanitised heritage trail. Railway remains, volunteer conservation, informal art and daily commuting all occupy the same space.

## A nature reserve built by neglect and care

Once railway maintenance stopped, grass, scrub and woodland colonised the embankments and cuttings. Haringey later designated Parkland Walk as a Local Nature Reserve. Council material records more than 200 species of wildflower across the reserve, while the Islington section includes the borough’s only acidic grassland.

This is not untouched nature. Its habitats developed on engineered ground and now require management. Volunteers cut back bramble, protect meadow areas and maintain wildlife features because complete abandonment would allow a smaller number of vigorous plants to dominate. The apparent wildness is partly the result of deliberate, patient care.

For another route where water, industry and urban nature refuse to separate neatly, the [Wandle Trail](/journal/wandle-trail-london-river-walk/) makes a useful south-London counterpart. Parkland Walk is shorter and more enclosed, but both reward attention to leftover infrastructure rather than a hunt for postcard scenery.

## Highgate is a break, not a secret passage

The southern path ends near the portals of the former Highgate tunnels. They are closed to the public. There is no legitimate route through them, and photographs that make the tunnels look inviting should not be treated as access advice.

To continue, climb back to street level and follow the signed or mapped connection around Highgate Wood towards Cranley Gardens. The northern section then returns to the railway alignment and leads towards Alexandra Palace. It is shorter, quieter and easier to miss. The change of scale makes it feel like an epilogue rather than a continuation.

Completing both sections gives the fuller story, but the main Finsbury Park–Highgate stretch works well on its own. If you are building a longer north-London day, Highgate can lead naturally towards the village or our practical guide to [Highgate Cemetery’s East and West sides](/journal/highgate-cemetery-east-west-guide/). Do not force every nearby attraction into the same outing: the walk is better when you leave time to stop at the platforms, examine the bridges and look back along the old track.

## How to walk it well

The reserve is open at all times, but ‘open’ does not mean evenly accessible. Some entrances use steep steps, the path is rough in places and wet weather can create mud and pools. The better ramps are useful, but they do not turn the whole route into a level path. Check the official access page for works or temporary diversions before making a special journey.

Use public transport and walk one way. Finsbury Park provides the simplest start for the southern section; Highgate, Archway, Crouch Hill and local buses offer several ways to leave or adapt the route. If you continue to Alexandra Palace, plan the street connection in advance rather than assuming the green path is continuous.

Most of all, resist treating Parkland Walk as a green shortcut. The pleasure lies in reading two landscapes at once: the woodland that exists now and the railway geometry still holding it in place.
dek: Between Finsbury Park and Highgate, trees have colonised a former railway without erasing it. Platforms, bridges and cuttings still dictate the route.
